title: Hepatic Encephalopathy: Diagnose Clinically, Find the Precipitant
bottomLine: Hepatic encephalopathy is a clinical syndrome in a patient with liver dysfunction/portosystemic shunting after alternative causes of altered mental status are considered. Do not use serum ammonia to diagnose, stage or monitor response; identify and treat the precipitant while using lactulose and selected rifaximin strategies appropriately.
recognize: Sleep-wake reversal, slowed thinking, confusion, asterixis and reduced consciousness can occur; covert disease may present with driving/work errors before obvious confusion.
Common precipitants include infection, GI bleeding, constipation, dehydration/overdiuresis, renal dysfunction, sedatives/opioids and electrolyte disturbance.
differentiate: Delirium from sepsis, medication toxicity, intracranial disease, hypoglycemia, alcohol withdrawal and other metabolic causes can coexist with cirrhosis.
Ammonia level does not reliably separate these conditions or measure clinical severity.
assessment: Assess mental status/baseline, infection, bleeding, bowel pattern, hydration, renal/electrolytes, medications, alcohol/withdrawal risk and focal neurologic findings.
workup: Use CBC, electrolytes/renal, glucose, infection/bleeding evaluation and imaging or toxicology only when indicated by the differential; ammonia is not required to establish a typical diagnosis.
management: Treat the precipitant and use lactulose titrated to clinical response/bowel output; add rifaximin for recurrent overt episodes according to hepatology guidance.
Protect airway and escalate severe altered consciousness, sepsis, GI bleed or other instability.
medicationSafety: Excess lactulose can cause dehydration/electrolyte disturbance and worsen encephalopathy risk.
Sedatives/opioids can precipitate or worsen encephalopathy and require careful review.
counselling: Teach caregivers early cognitive changes, bowel-regimen goals and medication/precipitant recognition; driving safety may require restriction.
followUp: Review precipitant prevention, recurrence, medication access/adherence and transplant/hepatology needs after an overt episode.
examTrap: Ordering serial ammonia levels to decide whether confusion is hepatic encephalopathy or whether lactulose is working.
oneLinePearl: Treat the patient and the precipitant; ammonia is not the encephalopathy score.

title: Acute Pancreatitis: Diagnose with Two-of-Three, Then Treat Severity and Cause
bottomLine: Acute pancreatitis is usually diagnosed when two of three are present: characteristic pain, lipase/amylase elevation consistent with pancreatitis, or characteristic imaging. Early care is supportive and severity/cause driven; routine antibiotics and routine early CT are not indicated in uncomplicated cases.
recognize: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting and lipase elevation are typical; gallstones and alcohol are common causes.
Persistent organ failure, hypotension, hypoxemia, oliguria or rising inflammatory burden indicates higher severity.
differentiate: Biliary colic/cholecystitis, perforated ulcer, mesenteric ischemia, MI and aortic disease can mimic upper-abdominal pain.
Lipase elevation alone without compatible symptoms does not automatically diagnose pancreatitis.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, hydration, oxygenation, pain, alcohol, gallstone symptoms, triglycerides, calcium, medications, pregnancy and organ failure.
workup: Use lipase, CBC/chemistry/renal/liver tests and ultrasound for suspected biliary cause; CT is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected complication/severe course rather than routine immediate imaging.
management: Provide goal-directed IV crystalloid, analgesia/antiemetics and early oral/enteral nutrition as tolerated; treat gallstone obstruction/cholangitis and other causes appropriately.
Do not give prophylactic antibiotics for sterile pancreatitis.
medicationSafety: Avoid excessive fixed-volume fluids in patients at risk of overload; reassess perfusion/respiratory status.
Drug-induced pancreatitis is a diagnosis requiring temporal/alternative-cause assessment, not reflex attribution.
counselling: Address alcohol, gallstone and triglyceride causes before discharge; recurrence prevention depends on etiology.
followUp: Ensure gallstone definitive management, lipid/alcohol care and reassessment of complications/nutrition when severe.
examTrap: Ordering routine contrast CT and prophylactic antibiotics on day one for a stable classic pancreatitis presentation.
oneLinePearl: Pancreatitis care is supportive early; severity and cause—not the lipase number—drive escalation.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology acute pancreatitis practice resources

title: Gallbladder Disease: Biliary Colic, Cholecystitis, Duct Stone, or Cholangitis?
bottomLine: Right-upper-quadrant pain is not one gallstone diagnosis. Distinguish transient biliary colic, persistent inflammatory cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis and infected obstruction/cholangitis because imaging, antibiotics, ERCP urgency and disposition differ.
recognize: Biliary colic is episodic postprandial RUQ/epigastric pain without sustained systemic inflammation.
Cholecystitis adds persistent pain/tenderness and inflammation; jaundice/cholestatic labs raise duct obstruction; fever/jaundice/RUQ pain with toxicity raises cholangitis.
differentiate: Pancreatitis, hepatitis, peptic disease, right-lower-lobe pneumonia and cardiac disease can mimic biliary pain.
A normal common-bile-duct diameter does not fully exclude an early/small duct stone when biochemical/clinical probability remains high.
assessment: Assess pain duration, fever, jaundice, vomiting, hemodynamics, pregnancy, pancreatitis symptoms and prior biliary events.
workup: Use RUQ ultrasound first for most gallbladder disease; use liver chemistry/lipase and MRCP/EUS/ERCP according to probability and need for therapy.
management: Cholecystitis requires surgical pathway/antibiotics when indicated; high-probability duct obstruction or cholangitis needs urgent biliary decompression planning.
Uncomplicated biliary colic receives analgesia and elective surgical referral rather than empiric prolonged antibiotics.
medicationSafety: Avoid delaying source control in cholangitis by repeatedly changing antibiotics.
Pregnancy changes imaging/procedure planning but serious biliary infection still requires timely care.
counselling: Teach return precautions for fever, jaundice, persistent pain/vomiting and explain why recurrent colic often leads to elective surgery.
followUp: Close the loop on surgical/biliary referral and recurrent-event prevention.
examTrap: Treating fever, jaundice and RUQ pain as uncomplicated biliary colic and arranging routine outpatient ultrasound.
oneLinePearl: Gallstones become urgent when inflammation, obstruction or infection enters the picture.

title: Colorectal Cancer Screening: Screen the Asymptomatic Patient, Diagnose the Symptomatic One
bottomLine: Colorectal screening applies to people without symptoms. Use the current provincial or territorial program and family-risk pathway; new rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, weight loss or change in bowel pattern requires diagnostic evaluation rather than simply ordering a screening FIT.
recognize: Average-risk screening ages and funded implementation vary by province/territory and are changing; Ontario lowered organized average-risk FIT eligibility to age 45 in July 2026.
Family history, hereditary syndromes and prior advanced polyps/cancer move patients outside average-risk screening.
differentiate: Screening FIT is not a rule-out test for symptomatic disease.
A positive FIT requires colonoscopic diagnostic follow-up; repeating FIT to see if it becomes negative is inappropriate.
assessment: Clarify symptoms first, age, anatomy, first-degree family history/age at diagnosis, prior colonoscopy/polyps, IBD and hereditary cancer features.
workup: Use the jurisdiction's current FIT/colonoscopy pathway for asymptomatic screening and colonoscopy/other diagnostic workup for symptoms or high-risk history.
management: Ensure abnormal screening tests are tracked to definitive colonoscopy/pathology and subsequent surveillance; address access barriers proactively.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulant/antiplatelet management only when an invasive procedure is planned; do not stop them solely for FIT.
counselling: Explain that screening intervals/programs differ across Canada and a new symptom changes the purpose from screening to diagnosis.
followUp: Own the result until diagnostic resolution and set recall using the final risk/pathology rather than generic intervals.
examTrap: Ordering a routine FIT for a patient with iron-deficiency anemia and rectal bleeding instead of initiating a diagnostic colorectal evaluation.
oneLinePearl: No symptoms means screening; symptoms mean diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology CRC resources

title: Colorectal Polyps: Let Pathology, Number, Size, Resection Quality, and Guideline Version Set Follow-Up
bottomLine: Post-polypectomy surveillance is not one universal interval. Use the final colonoscopy/pathology report, number/size/histology, completeness of resection, bowel preparation and current jurisdictional/endoscopy guidance; CAG's own post-polypectomy guideline remains on hold, so do not invent a Canada-wide interval table.
recognize: Advanced adenoma features, multiple adenomas, large serrated lesions, piecemeal resection and inadequate preparation can shorten follow-up.
A high-quality normal colonoscopy has a different risk pathway from an incomplete or poorly prepared examination.
differentiate: Screening recall intervals and post-polypectomy surveillance intervals are different questions.
Hereditary polyposis syndromes/IBD-associated dysplasia follow specialty surveillance rather than average post-polypectomy rules.
assessment: Retrieve the actual pathology and procedure report rather than relying on 'a polyp was removed'; document family history, quality/completeness and prior polyp burden.
workup: No additional test substitutes for the pathology/procedure details needed to set surveillance.
management: Assign follow-up using the current endoscopy/provincial guidance available to the clinician and document the rationale/ownership.
medicationSafety: Periendoscopic antithrombotic decisions depend on procedure bleeding risk and thrombotic risk, not the surveillance interval alone.
counselling: Give the patient the pathology result and exact next-step plan; avoid vague advice such as 'repeat in a few years'.
followUp: Use a recall system and update the interval if final pathology or guideline changes alter risk.
examTrap: Assigning the same five-year interval to every patient who has any polyp removed.
oneLinePearl: Polyp surveillance is pathology plus procedure quality plus current guidance—not a memorized one-size interval.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology guideline library — post-polypectomy guideline currently on hold

title: Chronic Constipation: Identify the Pattern Before Escalating Laxatives
bottomLine: Most chronic constipation can be diagnosed and treated clinically after medication/secondary-cause and alarm-feature review. Distinguish stool-consistency/slow-transit symptoms from outlet dysfunction; avoid routine colonoscopy in younger low-risk patients without alarm features.
recognize: Infrequent hard stools, straining, incomplete evacuation and manual maneuvers characterize constipation; normal stool frequency does not exclude outlet dysfunction.
Opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium channel blockers and metabolic/neurologic disease are common contributors.
differentiate: Pelvic-floor dyssynergia causes excessive straining, blockage sensation and incomplete evacuation and may not respond to more laxative.
New anemia, weight loss, bleeding or abrupt bowel change in a higher-risk patient requires structural evaluation.
assessment: Review stool form/frequency, evacuation symptoms, diet/fluid/activity, medications, neurologic/pelvic history, pregnancy and alarm features; perform rectal examination when outlet dysfunction is plausible.
workup: Use targeted CBC/TSH/calcium or other testing only when history suggests a secondary cause; colonoscopy is not routine solely for constipation in a younger low-risk patient.
management: Use fibre when appropriate and osmotic agents such as PEG as evidence-based first-line pharmacologic therapy; use secretagogues/prokinetics when indicated after simpler therapy.
Refer suspected pelvic-floor dysfunction for anorectal testing/biofeedback rather than endless laxative escalation.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic magnesium-containing laxatives in significant renal impairment without review; opioid-induced constipation may need a different strategy.
counselling: Set realistic stool/comfort goals and avoid reinforcing a belief that daily bowel movements are required for health.
followUp: Reassess response, adherence, outlet symptoms and emerging alarm features.
examTrap: Ordering colonoscopy for every young adult with chronic constipation and no alarm features—or adding more laxatives to clear pelvic-floor dyssynergia.
oneLinePearl: Constipation treatment works better when you know whether stool is slow, hard, or unable to exit.

title: Chronic Diarrhea: Classify the Stool, Then Target the Workup
bottomLine: Chronic diarrhea is a syndrome, not a test panel. Classify watery, fatty or inflammatory features; review medications/diet/travel and alarm signs; then target celiac, inflammatory, infectious, bile-acid, microscopic-colitis, malabsorption or endocrine testing to the pattern.
recognize: Nocturnal symptoms, blood, weight loss, anemia and inflammatory markers increase concern for organic disease.
Bile acid diarrhea is common and under-recognized after ileal disease/resection or cholecystectomy and can mimic IBS-D.
differentiate: Watery secretory diarrhea often persists during fasting; osmotic diarrhea improves with fasting; steatorrhea suggests fat malabsorption; inflammatory disease can cause blood/urgency/systemic features.
assessment: Assess duration, stool frequency/form/blood/fat, nocturnal pattern, weight, diet/sweeteners, medications including metformin/magnesium/PPIs, travel, antibiotics, surgery and immune risk.
workup: Use CBC, celiac serology, fecal inflammatory markers, stool microbiology and bile-acid/malabsorption evaluation selectively; colonoscopy with biopsies is needed for alarm features or suspected microscopic/inflammatory colitis.
management: Treat the cause and replace fluid/electrolyte/nutritional losses; avoid long-term empiric antibiotics without a defined infection.
medicationSafety: Antimotility agents are inappropriate in some severe inflammatory/invasive infections or toxic colitis presentations.
counselling: Avoid broad permanent dietary restriction before a diagnosis; use structured trials when diet is part of the hypothesis.
followUp: Close all abnormal test/pathology results and reassess the diagnosis when empiric treatment fails.
examTrap: Calling all chronic watery diarrhea IBS-D without considering bile acid diarrhea, celiac disease, microscopic colitis or medication effects.
oneLinePearl: Classify chronic diarrhea before you order the workup.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology bile acid diarrhea and IBS guidance

title: GI Bleeding: Stabilize First, Localize Second, Reverse Strategically
bottomLine: GI bleeding is a hemodynamic problem before it is an endoscopic diagnosis. Assess perfusion/airway, establish access and resuscitate appropriately, risk-stratify upper versus lower sources, manage antithrombotics according to bleeding/thrombotic risk, and obtain timely endoscopic source control.
recognize: Hematemesis/melena suggest upper GI bleeding; brisk upper bleeding can present as hematochezia.
Initial hemoglobin can be deceptively normal in acute blood loss; trend hemodynamics and hemoglobin after equilibration/resuscitation.
differentiate: Variceal bleeding has portal-hypertension-specific vasoactive/antibiotic/endoscopic management.
Lower-GI bleeding in an unstable patient may still be from a brisk upper source.
assessment: Assess ABCs, orthostasis/perfusion, bleeding amount, cirrhosis, NSAID/antiplatelet/anticoagulant use, prior ulcers/varices and comorbid cardiac disease.
workup: Use CBC, type/cross, renal/chemistry/coagulation as clinically useful and timely endoscopy/CTA/colonoscopy pathways according to location and instability.
management: Resuscitate with balanced crystalloid/blood as indicated and use restrictive transfusion principles in most stable patients while individualizing active shock/ischemia.
Use IV PPI for suspected high-risk nonvariceal upper bleeding; suspected variceal bleeding needs portal-hypertension-specific therapy and urgent endoscopy.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant reversal is reserved for clinically significant/life-threatening bleeding and is drug/risk specific; unnecessary reversal creates thrombosis risk.
Avoid NSAIDs after ulcer bleeding when possible.
counselling: After stabilization, explain source-specific recurrence prevention and antithrombotic restart plan.
followUp: Track pathology/H. pylori, repeat endoscopy when indicated, and ensure antithrombotic/iron management is closed-loop.
examTrap: Waiting for hemoglobin to fall before resuscitating an actively bleeding hypotensive patient.
oneLinePearl: GI bleed priorities are perfusion, source control and strategic medication reversal—in that order.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology upper-GI bleeding and periendoscopic antithrombotic guidance

title: Dysphagia: Oropharyngeal or Esophageal, Mechanical or Motility?
bottomLine: Dysphagia must first be localized. Coughing/choking at swallow initiation suggests oropharyngeal dysfunction and aspiration risk; food sticking after swallowing suggests esophageal disease. Progressive solids-first symptoms raise mechanical obstruction and warrant timely endoscopic evaluation.
recognize: Oropharyngeal disease causes difficulty initiating swallow, coughing, wet voice or nasal regurgitation.
Mechanical esophageal disease often begins with solids; motility disorders can affect solids and liquids from the start.
differentiate: Stroke/Parkinson/neuromuscular disease commonly causes oropharyngeal dysphagia.
Cancer/stricture/eosinophilic esophagitis versus achalasia/motility disease require different testing.
assessment: Ask where/when food sticks, solids vs liquids, progression, aspiration/chest infections, odynophagia, weight loss, reflux/allergy history and neurologic symptoms.
workup: Use speech/swallow assessment and videofluoroscopic/FEES pathways for oropharyngeal disease; use upper endoscopy for esophageal dysphagia/alarm features and manometry when motility disease remains likely after structural evaluation.
management: Protect swallowing/aspiration safety while the cause is evaluated; treat stricture/eosinophilic/reflux/motility or neurologic cause specifically.
medicationSafety: Pill formulations may be unsafe in severe dysphagia; do not crush modified-release/enteric-coated drugs without pharmacy review.
redFlags: Unable to handle secretions/food bolus impaction
counselling: Teach texture/position strategies only after swallowing assessment when aspiration risk is significant.
followUp: Close pathology/manometry/swallow-study results and nutritional/aspiration outcomes.
examTrap: Calling progressive solid-food dysphagia GERD and escalating a PPI without evaluating obstruction.
oneLinePearl: Localize dysphagia before you investigate it.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Esophageal Dysphagia guideline

title: Anorectal Symptoms: Do Not Let Hemorrhoids Explain Every Bleed
bottomLine: Rectal bleeding, pain, prolapse and pruritus require a focused anorectal examination and colorectal-risk assessment. Hemorrhoids are common but should not be used to explain bleeding without considering fissure, abscess, IBD, cancer and other causes.
recognize: Internal hemorrhoids typically cause painless bright-red bleeding/prolapse; thrombosed external hemorrhoids cause acute painful perianal swelling.
Anal fissure causes severe tearing pain with defecation; abscess causes constant pain, swelling and systemic infection risk.
differentiate: Fistula, Crohn disease, STI lesions, rectal prolapse and malignancy can mimic common benign anorectal disease.
assessment: Assess bleeding quantity, pain, bowel habits/straining, weight loss/anemia, family history, IBD, anticoagulants, pregnancy and perform external/DRE/anoscopy when appropriate.
workup: Escalate to colorectal/colonoscopy evaluation based on age/risk/alarm features rather than assuming hemorrhoids from bright-red blood alone.
management: Use fibre/stool-softening/defecation habit measures first for uncomplicated hemorrhoids and fissure; procedural/surgical referral depends on severity/persistence.
Drain anorectal abscess promptly; antibiotics alone are not definitive source control for a drainable abscess.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged topical corticosteroid/anesthetic use without reassessment; anticoagulants increase bleeding impact but do not establish the source.
counselling: Teach fibre, hydration/straining reduction and when persistent bleeding needs reassessment even with known hemorrhoids.
followUp: Confirm resolution or investigate persistent bleeding/pain and close any colorectal referral.
examTrap: Diagnosing hemorrhoids from bright-red rectal blood without performing an anorectal examination or considering colorectal cancer risk.
oneLinePearl: Hemorrhoids are common; unexplained rectal bleeding still deserves a source.

title: Abdominal Pain: Disposition Before Diagnostic Perfection
bottomLine: Acute abdominal pain is first a stability/disposition problem. Identify shock, peritonitis, pregnancy emergencies, obstruction, ischemia, perforation and vascular disease before pursuing a perfectly specific diagnosis; analgesia should not be withheld while evaluating serious disease.
recognize: Older/immunocompromised patients may have serious disease with muted tenderness/fever.
Pain out of proportion raises mesenteric ischemia; rigid/peritoneal abdomen raises perforation/inflammation; pregnancy possibility changes the differential immediately.
differentiate: Cardiac, pulmonary, metabolic, urinary and gynecologic disease can present as abdominal pain.
Location/migration and associated symptoms are more useful than pain score alone.
assessment: Assess ABCs/hemodynamics, onset/location/migration, vomiting/stool/urine/bleeding/fever, surgery, medications/anticoagulants and pregnancy possibility; perform focused relevant pelvic/testicular/cardiopulmonary exam.
workup: Use pregnancy test, CBC/chemistry/liver/lipase/urinalysis, ECG/troponin and imaging based on differential; ultrasound is preferred when it answers a biliary/pelvic/pregnancy question without radiation.
management: Give appropriate analgesia/antiemetics and resuscitation while testing; urgent surgical/ED pathway for shock, peritonitis, ischemia, perforation, ectopic or compromised obstruction.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs can worsen GI bleeding/renal disease; opioids require sedation/respiratory reassessment but need not be withheld solely to preserve exam findings.
counselling: For safe outpatient care, give explicit return precautions for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, bleeding, syncope or inability to hydrate.
followUp: Close pending imaging/labs and reassess evolving pain when diagnosis remains provisional.
examTrap: Withholding analgesia until the surgeon examines the patient—or choosing a benign diagnosis before deciding whether the patient is safe to go home.
oneLinePearl: In abdominal pain, disposition comes before diagnostic elegance.

title: Liver Tests in GI Disease: Injury, Cholestasis, and Synthetic Function Are Different Axes
bottomLine: AST/ALT primarily reflect hepatocellular injury, ALP/bilirubin help identify cholestasis/handling, and INR/albumin contribute synthetic information in context. Do not diagnose liver failure from aminotransferases or use falling AST/ALT as proof of recovery when INR, bilirubin, glucose or mental status worsen.
recognize: AST is less liver-specific than ALT; ALP can arise from liver, bone or placenta; GGT can support hepatobiliary origin but is nonspecific.
Albumin changes slowly and is affected by inflammation, nutrition and renal/GI loss.
differentiate: Hepatocellular, cholestatic and mixed patterns have different etiologic pathways.
Bilirubin can rise in both hepatocellular and cholestatic disease and should be interpreted with fractionation/pattern.
assessment: Assess symptoms, medication/supplement/alcohol exposure, hemodynamics, pregnancy, infection/viral risk and signs of decompensation.
workup: Classify the biochemical pattern first, then order targeted viral/autoimmune/metabolic/toxicology or ultrasound/other imaging.
management: Treat the cause and escalate synthetic failure, encephalopathy, hypoglycemia, obstructed infection or rapid deterioration urgently.
medicationSafety: Mild stable transaminase abnormalities do not automatically require stopping beneficial medications; suspected severe drug-induced liver injury requires prompt review.
counselling: Explain why a 'liver panel' contains tests that answer different questions.
followUp: Trend the abnormalities that answer the clinical question and complete cause/fibrosis evaluation for persistent disease.
examTrap: Declaring acute liver injury improved because AST/ALT fall while INR and mental status worsen.
oneLinePearl: Read liver tests by job, not as one score.

title: GI Tumour Markers: Monitoring Tools, Not Cancer Screening Tests
bottomLine: CEA, CA 19-9, AFP and other tumour markers are not general screening tests for asymptomatic people and rarely establish a GI cancer diagnosis by themselves. Use them only in the specific diagnosed/suspected cancer contexts where they change staging, surveillance or treatment response.
recognize: CEA can be elevated by smoking/inflammation and is mainly used in selected colorectal-cancer follow-up contexts.
CA 19-9 can rise with benign cholestasis and some people do not produce it; AFP has liver/germ-cell contexts but is not a standalone HCC screen.
differentiate: A marker is not a substitute for imaging, endoscopy/pathology or organized screening.
A rising marker can prompt investigation in a previously diagnosed cancer but does not prove recurrence by itself.
assessment: Ask what cancer context/question the marker is intended to answer; if there is no specific action attached to the result, do not order it as a fishing expedition.
workup: Use guideline-directed imaging/endoscopy/pathology and organized screening; use tumour markers only as adjuncts in their validated setting.
management: Investigate a clinically meaningful change in the context of disease history rather than treating the marker number.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary invasive tests solely from one nonspecific marker elevation without pretest context.
redFlags: Rising marker in known cancer with clinical concern
counselling: Explain that tumour markers are imperfect and are not a simple blood test to rule cancer in or out.
followUp: If a marker is used longitudinally, use the same disease-specific protocol and close abnormal results to definitive evaluation.
examTrap: Ordering CEA or CA 19-9 to screen an asymptomatic average-risk adult for cancer.
oneLinePearl: Tumour markers support a cancer pathway; they do not create the diagnosis.

title: Endoscopy: Ask a Clinical Question, Then Own the Result
bottomLine: Endoscopy is indicated when the result can diagnose/treat a meaningful GI problem: bleeding, dysphagia/alarm symptoms, selected dyspepsia, IBD assessment, cancer screening/surveillance, polyp removal or other defined indications. It should not be ordered reflexively for low-risk symptoms when a noninvasive pathway is preferred.
recognize: Upper endoscopy can diagnose/treat bleeding, obstruction/stricture and mucosal disease; colonoscopy is diagnostic/therapeutic after positive FIT, symptoms, higher-risk screening or surveillance indications.
differentiate: Screening colonoscopy, diagnostic colonoscopy and post-polypectomy surveillance are different clinical purposes.
Routine repeat endoscopy without a new indication adds procedure risk and low value.
assessment: Define the clinical question, alarm features, cardiopulmonary/sedation risk, prior endoscopy/pathology, anticoagulants/antiplatelets and ability to complete preparation/follow-up.
workup: Use the least invasive effective diagnostic pathway when appropriate; ensure pre-procedure medication/preparation management follows current endoscopy guidance.
management: Urgent endoscopy for significant bleeding/food bolus or other emergencies; elective timing for stable diagnostic/surveillance indications.
Assign explicit ownership of pathology, biopsy and surveillance plans.
medicationSafety: Periendoscopic anticoagulant/antiplatelet interruption depends on both procedure bleeding risk and thrombotic risk; avoid universal hold rules.
counselling: Explain the purpose, sedation/prep risks, what happens with abnormal pathology and who will communicate results.
followUp: Track pathology and procedure recommendations to completion; do not treat 'procedure done' as the end of the diagnostic episode.
examTrap: Ordering an upper endoscopy for uncomplicated low-risk dyspepsia without alarm features before using the recommended noninvasive/empiric pathway.
oneLinePearl: A good endoscopy order begins with a question and ends with closed-loop follow-up.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology guideline library/endoscopy guidance

title: Nutrition Assessment: Diagnose the Deficit Before You Prescribe the Supplement
bottomLine: Nutrition assessment integrates intake, weight trajectory, function/body composition, GI losses, disease burden and micronutrient risk. A normal BMI does not exclude malnutrition, and supplements should target a defined need rather than replace adequate food/enteral nutrition automatically.
recognize: Unintentional weight loss, low intake, muscle loss, weakness, edema, poor wound healing and recurrent illness can signal malnutrition.
Obesity can coexist with protein-calorie or micronutrient malnutrition.
differentiate: Inflammation-related cachexia, malabsorption, food insecurity, dysphagia and eating disorders require different interventions.
Low albumin is strongly influenced by inflammation and should not be used alone to diagnose malnutrition.
assessment: Use recent weight change, intake, functional status, physical exam/muscle stores, food access, swallowing, GI symptoms, medications, alcohol and disease-specific needs.
workup: Order iron/B12/folate/vitamin D/electrolytes or other micronutrients only when risk/clinical features support them; monitor refeeding electrolytes in high-risk severe malnutrition.
management: Use oral food fortification/supplements when adequate; prefer enteral feeding when the GI tract works but oral intake is unsafe/insufficient; parenteral nutrition is reserved for nonfunctional/inaccessible GI tract or specific indications.
medicationSafety: Micronutrient megadoses can be toxic/interact with drugs; refeeding can cause dangerous phosphate, potassium and magnesium shifts.
counselling: Use culturally appropriate, affordable food plans and avoid moralizing weight/intake; involve dietitians and social resources.
followUp: Track weight/function/intake and disease-specific laboratory response rather than supplement use alone.
examTrap: Diagnosing or excluding malnutrition from BMI or albumin alone.
oneLinePearl: Nutrition care starts with trajectory and function, not a single lab or body-size label.

title: Short Bowel Syndrome: Replace What Is Lost, Preserve What Remains
bottomLine: Short bowel syndrome causes malabsorption and fluid/electrolyte/nutrient loss based on remaining bowel length and anatomy. Management prioritizes hydration/sodium, nutrition, anti-diarrheal/acid-reduction strategies, micronutrient replacement and intestinal adaptation, with intestinal-failure specialist care when parenteral support is required.
recognize: High stool/ostomy output, dehydration, weight loss and deficiencies can follow major small-bowel resection.
Ileal loss affects bile salts/B12; absence of colon reduces fluid/energy salvage; anatomy predicts risk better than the label alone.
differentiate: High-output stoma from infection, obstruction or medication can mimic/worsen short-bowel losses.
Kidney injury and stones can result from chronic dehydration or altered oxalate handling.
assessment: Document residual anatomy, stool/ostomy output, urine output, weight, hydration, diet, renal function, electrolytes/magnesium, B12/fat-soluble vitamins, liver/bone status and parenteral access complications.
workup: Trend fluid/electrolyte/nutrient status and investigate abrupt output increases for infection/obstruction/medication causes rather than simply increasing nutrition support.
management: Use individualized oral/enteral nutrition to promote adaptation, oral rehydration/sodium strategies, antidiarrheals and acid suppression when indicated; provide parenteral fluid/nutrition when enteral absorption cannot meet needs.
Specialist intestinal-rehabilitation programs determine candidacy for trophic therapy, surgical reconstruction or transplant.
medicationSafety: Drug absorption can be unreliable after extensive resection; extended-release/enteric formulations may fail and dosing requires drug-specific review.
Central venous nutrition carries bloodstream infection/thrombosis/liver risks.
counselling: Teach urine/output monitoring, oral rehydration rather than plain-water overuse in high-output states, medication absorption issues and line safety.
followUp: Coordinate GI/nutrition/pharmacy monitoring of hydration, micronutrients, renal/liver/bone health and parenteral-support reduction when adaptation permits.
examTrap: Telling a high-output short-bowel patient to drink unlimited plain water, which can worsen sodium balance and output.
oneLinePearl: Short bowel care is anatomy-specific fluid and nutrient replacement while the intestine adapts.
